sql.nudge: When a date string `'2026-01-31'` is cast to a TIMESTAMP, what time of day does it default to?

choices.text: `BETWEEN` in SQL is exclusive of both endpoints.
String dates cannot be compared to TIMESTAMP columns in SQL.

sql.examRule: Never use `BETWEEN` with date literals on TIMESTAMP columns—it cuts off the final day at midnight. Use half-open ranges: `>= '2026-01-01' AND < '2026-02-01'`.

sql.goal: Return the total number of registered accounts in `users`, including accounts that haven't verified an email yet.
lines: -- Unverified users with email = NULL are missing from the count!
sql.nudge: How does `COUNT(column_name)` treat rows where `column_name` is NULL?

choices.text: `COUNT(email)` skips every row where `email` is NULL; use `COUNT(*)` to count all rows.
`COUNT(email)` only counts distinct email addresses.
`AS total_users` requires a `GROUP BY` clause.

sql.examRule: `COUNT(*)` counts every row, whereas `COUNT(col)` silently ignores NULL values in `col`.

python.goal: Use default timeout 30 only when `timeout` is `None`, while still allowing `timeout=0` (no wait).
python.nudge: In Python, `0`, `""`, and `[]` are all falsy. How do you check specifically for `None`?

choices.text: `not timeout` treats `0` as falsy and replaces it with 30; check `if timeout is None:` explicitly.
`return 30` overrides `timeout` even when `timeout` is 10.
Python functions cannot accept `0` as an argument.

python.examRule: Never use `if not x:` when `0`, `False`, or `""` are valid inputs. Check `if x is None:` explicitly.

python.goal: Return True if a 200,000-element list contains any duplicate values, in O(N) time.
python.nudge: What is the time complexity of `x in seen` when `seen` is a Python `list` vs a `set`?

choices.text: Membership lookup `x in list` is O(N), making the loop O(N²) TLE; use `seen = set()` and `seen.add(x)` for O(1) lookups.
`seen.append(x)` sorts the list on every insertion.
`if x in seen` only checks the first and last element of a list.

python.examRule: In Python OAs, `x in list` is O(N) linear scan, whereas `x in set` is O(1) average hash lookup. Use a `set` for membership tracking.

python.goal: Filter out IEEE 754 `NaN` values from a list of sensor readings.
lines: return [v for v in vals if v != float("nan")]
# float("nan") values are STILL in the returned list!
python.nudge: Under IEEE 754 rules, what does `NaN != NaN` evaluate to?

accept: return [v for v in vals if not math.isnan(v)]

choices.text: In IEEE 754, `NaN != NaN` is always `True`, so `v != float("nan")` keeps every NaN; use `not math.isnan(v)`.
`float("nan")` creates a string instead of a floating-point number.
List comprehensions cannot filter floating-point numbers.

python.examRule: `NaN` is never equal to anything—including itself (`NaN == NaN` is False, `NaN != NaN` is True). Always detect it with `math.isnan(v)`.

cpp.nudge: Look closely at the operator inside `if (status = 200)`.

choices.text: Single `=` assigns 200 to `status` and evaluates to 200 (truthy); use `==` for comparison.
200 overflows a signed `int` in C++.
`status` must be declared `const` before comparing to 200.

cpp.examRule: In C++, `if (a = b)` is legal assignment, not comparison. Compile with `-Wall` and always double-check `==`.

cpp.goal: Sort a vector of integers in descending order without causing undefined behavior on equal elements.
lines: // Segfaults on large inputs with many duplicate values!
cpp.nudge: `std::sort` requires a strict weak ordering: what must `comp(x, x)` return for equal elements?

choices.text: `a >= b` returns `true` when `a == b`, violating strict weak ordering and causing out-of-bounds UB in `std::sort`; use `a > b`.
Lambdas cannot be passed as comparators to `std::sort`.
`v.end()` points to the last valid element, causing an off-by-one error.

cpp.examRule: C++ `std::sort` comparators MUST satisfy strict weak ordering (`comp(x, x)` must be `false`). Never use `<=` or `>=` in a comparator—use `<` or `>`.

cpp.goal: Link two heap-allocated nodes together without causing a permanent memory leak when they go out of scope.
lines: // a->next = b; b->prev = a; never frees either Node!
cpp.nudge: If `a` holds a `shared_ptr` to `b` and `b` holds a `shared_ptr` to `a`, can their reference counts ever reach 0?

choices.text: Two mutual `std::shared_ptr` links create a reference cycle whose count never drops to 0; make the back-pointer `std::weak_ptr<Node>`.
`struct` members default to `private` and cannot be destroyed.
`std::shared_ptr` does not free memory automatically in C++.

cpp.examRule: Mutual `std::shared_ptr` references create reference cycles that leak memory forever. Break cycles using `std::weak_ptr` for non-owning back-links.

java.goal: Split an IPv4 address like "192.168.0.1" into its 4 numeric parts.
lines: // Returns an empty array [] instead of ["192", "168", "0", "1"]!
java.nudge: `String.split()` takes a Regular Expression, not a literal delimiter. What does `.` match in regex?

choices.text: `String.split()` interprets `.` as a regex wildcard matching every character; escape it as `ip.split("\\.")`.
`String.split()` returns a `List<String>` rather than `String[]`.
Periods cannot appear inside Java string literals.

java.examRule: Java's `String.split(regex)` takes a regular expression. Escape regex metacharacters like `.` or `|` with `"\\."` or `Pattern.quote(".")`.

java.goal: Create a `BigDecimal` representing the exact decimal value 0.1 without binary floating-point noise.
java.nudge: What is the exact value of the `double` literal `0.1` before it even reaches the `BigDecimal` constructor?

choices.text: `new BigDecimal(double)` captures the inexact binary float representation; use `new BigDecimal("0.1")` or `BigDecimal.valueOf(0.1)`.
`BigDecimal` only supports integer values, not decimals.
`BigDecimal` rounds all numbers up to 1.0 by default.

java.examRule: Never pass a `double` to `new BigDecimal(double)`—it preserves binary float inaccuracy. Use `new BigDecimal("0.1")` or `BigDecimal.valueOf(0.1)`.

java.goal: Return the largest double in a non-empty array that may contain only negative numbers.
java.nudge: Unlike `Integer.MIN_VALUE`, is `Double.MIN_VALUE` negative or positive in Java?

choices.text: `Double.MIN_VALUE` is the smallest POSITIVE double (4.9e-324), not negative; initialize with `Double.NEGATIVE_INFINITY` or `-Double.MAX_VALUE`.
Comparing negative doubles with `>` is reversed in Java.
`Double.MIN_VALUE` is equal to `NaN`.

java.examRule: Classic Java OA trap: `Double.MIN_VALUE` is POSITIVE (`4.9e-324`). For the lowest possible double, use `Double.NEGATIVE_INFINITY` or `-Double.MAX_VALUE`.

sql.goal: Return all orders whose status is NOT 'CANCELLED', including newly created orders where status is still NULL.
lines: -- Orders with status = NULL are silently dropped!
sql.nudge: In SQL three-valued logic, does `NULL != 'CANCELLED'` evaluate to TRUE or UNKNOWN?

choices.text: `NULL != 'CANCELLED'` evaluates to UNKNOWN, dropping NULL rows; use `WHERE status IS NULL OR status != 'CANCELLED'` (or `IS DISTINCT FROM`).
`!=` is invalid SQL syntax and always returns 0 rows.
String comparisons in `WHERE` are case-insensitive only when using `<>`.

sql.examRule: Inequality (`!=` or `<>`) never matches `NULL` in SQL. Always handle nullable columns with `IS NULL OR col != ...` or `IS DISTINCT FROM`.

sql.goal: Query all 2026 orders while allowing the database to use the B-Tree index on `created_at`.
lines: -- Triggers a full table scan on 50M rows despite index on created_at!
sql.nudge: What happens to a B-Tree index when you wrap the indexed column inside a function like `YEAR(...)`?

choices.text: Wrapping `created_at` in `YEAR()` makes the predicate non-SARGable and disables the B-Tree index; use a range `>= '2026-01-01' AND < '2027-01-01'`.
`YEAR(created_at)` returns a string `'2026'`, which cannot equal integer `2026`.
B-Tree indexes cannot be used on `SELECT` queries without `ORDER BY`.

sql.examRule: Keep indexed columns bare on one side of the comparison (SARGable). Wrapping a column in `YEAR(col)` or `LOWER(col)` prevents standard B-Tree index seeks.

sql.goal: Compute a strict row-by-row running sum of PnL, even when two trades share the exact same `trade_date`.
lines: SUM(pnl) OVER (ORDER BY trade_date) AS running_pnl
-- Same-day trades jump to the same combined total!
sql.nudge: When you write `OVER (ORDER BY col)` without specifying a frame, does SQL default to `ROWS` or `RANGE`?

choices.text: `OVER (ORDER BY trade_date)` defaults to `RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`, grouping peer ties together; add `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`.
`SUM()` cannot be used with `OVER (ORDER BY ...)` without `PARTITION BY`.
`ORDER BY trade_date` sorts the entire table in descending order by default.

sql.examRule: In SQL window functions, `ORDER BY` defaults to a `RANGE` frame (which includes all peer ties). Specify `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` for strict row-by-row running totals.

python.goal: Wrap `item` inside a 1-element tuple and return it.
lines: # type(wrap_tuple(42)) is int instead of tuple!
python.nudge: In Python, parentheses alone just group an expression. What character actually defines a 1-element tuple?

choices.text: `(item)` is just a parenthesized value; a 1-element tuple requires a trailing comma: `(item,)`.
Python tuples must contain at least 2 elements.
Returning a tuple requires calling `tuple(item)` even for integers.

python.examRule: In Python, the comma—not the parentheses—creates a tuple. Always write `(x,)` for a single-element tuple.

python.goal: Remove only the trailing ".py" extension from a Python filename.
python.nudge: Does `str.strip(chars)` remove an exact substring, or any individual character in the set `'.', 'p', 'y'`?

choices.text: `strip(".py")` strips ANY leading or trailing '.', 'p', or 'y' characters; use `filename.removesuffix(".py")`.
`strip()` only removes whitespace and ignores its argument.
`strip(".py")` removes `".py"` from the middle of the string too.

python.examRule: `str.strip(chars)` treats its argument as a SET of characters to strip from both ends. Use `removeprefix()` / `removesuffix()` (Python 3.9+) for exact substrings.

python.goal: Pause an async worker coroutine for 1 second without freezing the entire asyncio event loop.
lines: # Blocks all other concurrent coroutines for 1 full second!
python.nudge: Does `time.sleep(1)` yield control back to the `asyncio` event loop, or block the OS thread?

choices.text: `time.sleep(1)` blocks the entire single-threaded event loop; use `await asyncio.sleep(1)` to yield control.
`async def` functions cannot return string values.
Importing `asyncio` and `time` on the same line disables async scheduling.

python.examRule: Never call blocking I/O or `time.sleep()` inside an `async def` coroutine—it freezes the entire event loop. Use `await asyncio.sleep()`.

cpp.goal: Return the number of elements in the passed C-style integer array.
lines: // Always returns 2 on 64-bit systems regardless of array length!
cpp.nudge: When `int arr[]` is a function parameter in C++, what type does `arr` actually decay to?

choices.text: Array parameters decay to `int*`, so `sizeof(arr)` returns the pointer size (8 bytes) instead of the array size; use `std::span` or pass length.
`sizeof(arr[0])` returns 0 because `arr` is uninitialized.
`sizeof` only works on `std::vector`, not raw arrays.

cpp.examRule: C-style array parameters always decay to pointers (`int*`). Never use `sizeof(arr)` inside a function—pass `std::span<const int>` or `const std::vector<int>&`.

cpp.goal: Pop and return the SMALLEST integer from a priority queue of incoming values.
cpp.nudge: Unlike Python's `heapq` (min-heap), is C++'s `std::priority_queue<int>` a min-heap or a max-heap by default?

choices.text: `std::priority_queue<int>` is a MAX-heap by default (`std::less`); use `std::priority_queue<int, std::vector<int>, std::greater<int>>` for a min-heap.
`pq.top()` returns the last element inserted rather than the smallest.
Constructing a `priority_queue` from iterators skips sorting.

cpp.examRule: C++ `std::priority_queue` is a MAX-heap by default (opposite of Python's `heapq`). Specify `std::greater<int>` as the 3rd template argument for a min-heap.

cpp.goal: Keep a reference to the first element of `v`, append 99, and return the first element safely.
lines: // Heap-use-after-free under ASan when v reallocates!
cpp.nudge: If `v.push_back(99)` exceeds `v.capacity()`, where does the old buffer that `first` references go?

choices.text: `v.push_back(99)` can reallocate `v`'s internal buffer, freeing the old memory and leaving `int& first` as a dangling reference (UB).
`v[0]` returns a temporary rvalue that cannot bind to `int&`.
`push_back(99)` overwrites index 0 when the vector is full.

cpp.examRule: Any `std::vector` operation that may reallocate (`push_back`, `emplace_back`, `resize`) invalidates all existing pointers, references, and iterators into that vector.

java.goal: Return a non-negative bucket index in `[0, buckets - 1]` for any possible 32-bit `hashCode()`.
lines: public int bucketIndex(int hash, int buckets) {
java.nudge: In two's complement 32-bit arithmetic, what does `Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE)` return?

choices.text: `Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE)` overflows and returns `Integer.MIN_VALUE` (negative!); use `Math.floorMod(hash, buckets)` or `(hash & 0x7fffffff) % buckets`.
The `%` operator always returns a negative number when `buckets` is even.
`Math.abs()` returns a `double` that cannot be used with `%`.

java.examRule: `Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE)` is still negative (`-2147483648`). For non-negative hash bucketing, use `Math.floorMod(hash, buckets)` or `(hash & 0x7fffffff) % buckets`.

java.goal: Store a user record under a `List<String>` key, then reliably look it up again.
lines: // val is null even though key is in the map!
java.nudge: When `key.add("B")` mutates the list, what happens to `key.hashCode()` compared to the bucket where it was stored?

choices.text: Mutating a key after `put()` changes its `hashCode()`, so `get(key)` searches the wrong bucket and returns `null`.
`HashMap` forbids `List<String>` as a key type at runtime.
`cache.put(key, 100)` deletes `key` after reading its value.

java.examRule: Never mutate an object's `hashCode()`-bearing fields after inserting it as a `HashMap` key or `HashSet` element. Use immutable keys like `List.of(...)` or `record`s.

java.goal: Count matching items in a `Stream<String>` and also grab the first matching item.
lines: // Throws IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon!
java.nudge: Can a Java `Stream` be consumed by more than one terminal operation (`count()`, `findFirst()`)?

choices.text: Java Streams are single-use; `s.count()` closes the stream, so calling `s.findFirst()` throws `IllegalStateException`.
`findFirst()` cannot be called on a filtered `Stream<String>`.
`s.count()` mutates and empties the underlying `items` list.

java.examRule: A Java `Stream` can only run ONE terminal operation. Collect to a `List` first or create a fresh `items.stream()` for each pass.

sql.goal: Return the decimal conversion rate (e.g., 0.25) from two integer columns `orders` and `visits`.
lines: -- Returns 0 for every campaign in Postgres / SQL Server!
sql.nudge: What happens when you divide two `INTEGER` columns in Postgres or SQL Server?

choices.text: Integer division truncates `orders / visits` to 0; multiply by `1.0` or cast one operand to `FLOAT`/`NUMERIC` first.
The `/` operator is not supported in `SELECT` clauses.
Column aliases like `AS conv_rate` force integer rounding.

sql.examRule: In Postgres, SQL Server, and SQLite, `int / int` performs integer division and truncates to 0. Multiply by `1.0` or `CAST` to `NUMERIC`/`FLOAT`.

sql.goal: List EVERY product in the catalog along with its total units sold (including unsold products).
lines: JOIN sales s ON p.id = s.product_id
-- Unsold products disappear from the report!
sql.nudge: What kind of join is a bare `JOIN` in SQL, and what does it do to products with zero matching rows in `sales`?

choices.text: `JOIN` defaults to `INNER JOIN`, which drops products with no matching sales; use `LEFT JOIN`.
`COALESCE(SUM(s.qty), 0)` removes rows whose sum is 0.
Grouping by both `p.id` and `p.name` excludes unsold products.

sql.examRule: A bare `JOIN` is always an `INNER JOIN`. Use `LEFT JOIN` whenever you need to preserve parent rows that have zero child matches.

sql.goal: Compute revenue per click for every ad, returning NULL safely when an ad has 0 clicks.
lines: -- Crashes the entire query with DivisionByZeroError when clicks = 0!
sql.nudge: Which standard SQL function turns `0` into `NULL` so division returns `NULL` instead of crashing?

choices.text: Dividing by `clicks = 0` throws a runtime error; wrap the denominator in `NULLIF(clicks, 0)` so zero becomes NULL.
SQL automatically converts division by zero into `0` in all databases.
`COALESCE(clicks, 0)` prevents division by zero.

sql.examRule: Always guard SQL denominators with `NULLIF(denom, 0)` so zero denominators evaluate cleanly to `NULL` instead of crashing the query.
